definition: Proliferate means to increase rapidly in number — to multiply, with new ones appearing faster and faster.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word proliferate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know proliferate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Ten years ago the block had one coffee shop; today espresso bars proliferate on every corner, sometimes three to an intersection.
Multiply is milder than proliferate: numbers multiply at any pace, even a stately one, while to proliferate is to multiply with the throttle open — fast, everywhere, and hard to stop.
Mushroom goes further than proliferate — what proliferates climbs steeply, but what mushrooms seems to double overnight, springing up whole before anyone has counted the first batch.

To burgeon is to grow and flourish quickly — a bud swelling into bloom. Burgeoning is about vigorous growth in size or strength; proliferate is strictly about number: new units appearing, the count climbing. A single business can burgeon; only many of something can proliferate.

To abound is to exist in great plenty — it names the crowded state after the growth has happened. Proliferate names the process itself: things abound once they have proliferated. If the count is still climbing, proliferate is the word.

Proliferate means to increase rapidly in number — to multiply, with new ones appearing faster and faster.
When the city dropped its food-cart licensing fee, carts proliferated overnight — four the first spring, forty by the next — until the health department begged for more inspectors.
Proliferate is more exact than 'grow' or 'spread': it says the number of separate things is climbing fast — four carts becoming forty — as if the things were breeding.
One thing getting larger never proliferates; only a rising count does.
Proliferate needs a head-count: many separate things multiplying, the tally climbing.
One thing growing bigger or fiercer doesn't proliferate — it swells, spreads, or escalates.
The word often carries a wary edge, used for things multiplying faster than anyone quite wants: committees, regulations, weapons programs.

The first rental scooters appeared outside the university in March -- a single rack of ten, lime green.
By August they had proliferated past any office's ability to map them: four competing companies, eleven thousand scooters, and sidewalks in some districts nearly impassable.
City hall had planned to study the pilot for a year.
Instead it spent the summer fielding complaints and towing scooters out of fountains.
The council's eventual ordinance capped fleets, created parking corrals, and fined companies for every unit found blocking a curb ramp.
Transit researchers shrugged at the chaos; in their data, they noted, every new mobility technology spreads first and gets governed second.
